docs.title: pyStreamPU
docs.text:
pyStreamPU is the Python interface of StreamPU, a C++ Domain Specific Embedded Language (DSEL) for building high-throughput, low-latency streaming applications on multicore CPUs.

With the streampu package you build, from Python, a data-flow graph of tasks exchanging data through sockets, and let the StreamPU runtime execute it, sequentially or in parallel. The bindings are generated with pybind11.

import streampu as spu

x = spu.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=spu.uint8)
y = spu.array([4, 5, 6], dtype=spu.uint8)
print(x + y)  # [[5 7 9]]
The graph built by x + y: the data sockets of two Array modules are bound to the inputs of a Binaryop<add> module.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This page explains the model behind StreamPU and how it appears in Python. The tutorial shows the same notions through examples.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
StreamPU describes a streaming application as a data-flow graph:

Notion Role Python class Socket holds data exchanged between tasks spu.Socket Task a processing step: reads input sockets, writes output sockets spu.Task Module groups tasks that share parameters and possibly a state spu.Module and its subclasses Sequence a graph of bound tasks, executed on one or several threads spu.Sequence Pipeline a graph split into stages that run concurrently spu.Pipeline Two modules, their tasks and sockets, and a binding between them.

For example, spu.incrementer(8) is a module with a task increment, which reads the socket in and writes the socket out. Each built-in module wraps a C++ class of StreamPU; the Python objects give direct access to the C++ objects.

docs.title: Sockets
docs.text:
A socket has a name, a data type (dtype), a number of elements and belongs to a task. These properties are fixed when the task is created.

Its direction says how the task uses it:

Direction spu.Socket.directions The task… input IN reads the data output OUT writes the data forward FWD reads and modifies the data in place

Every task also has an output socket named status, where it writes its return code.

docs.title: Data, frames and NumPy
docs.text:
The data of a socket is stored in a C++ buffer. Its numpy attribute is a NumPy array that shares this buffer: modifying the array modifies the socket, and conversely. In the same way, spu.array(np_array) does not copy np_array.

This array is 2D, with one row per frame. A task processes n_frames frames per execution (1 by default), which is set on the modules or on a whole sequence with n_frames. Processing several frames at once reduces the overhead of each execution.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
A task is executed by its exec() method, or by calling it. Its main attributes are:

Attribute Meaning name, module name of the task and module that owns it sockets, inputs, outputs, forwards its sockets, all or by direction debug print the content of the sockets at each execution stats, n_calls, avg_duration… execution statistics (see Measuring performance)

The sockets of a task are reached by name: task["out"], task.out, or module["task::out"] from its module.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
A module is created by a factory function (spu.incrementer, spu.source_random, spu.relayer…) or by a class (spu.Stateless, your own C++ classes…). Its main attributes are name, tasks (list of its tasks) and n_frames. Its tasks are reached by name: module["increment"] or module.increment. spu.help(module) displays its tasks and their sockets.

Modules come in two kinds:

  • stateful modules keep data between executions (a source that reads a file, a random generator…). To run on several threads they must know how to copy themselves, which is not always possible;
  • stateless modules (spu.Stateless) only depend on their input sockets and are cloned automatically.

Both kinds can be written in Python (see Writing a module in Python).

docs.title: Binding
docs.text:
Binding an input (or forward) socket to an output (or forward) socket of another task makes them share the same data: the second task reads what the first one wrote, without copy. Bindings define the edges of the graph.

There are three equivalent ways to bind sockets:

inc["increment::in"] = src["generate::out_data"]   # assignment
inc["increment::in"].bind(src["generate::out_data"])
out = inc.increment(src["generate::out_data"])     # call

A task can also be bound to a socket or to another task (task.bind(...)) to force an execution order without exchanging data.

docs.title: Immediate execution and replay
docs.text:
Calling a task, or using an operator on sockets (x + 1, x[::2]…), does two things:

  1. it binds the sockets of the task to the arguments;
  2. it executes the task once, so that the result is immediately available.

This makes it possible to explore the data interactively. The bindings stay in place: step by step, these calls build a graph. A sequence then captures this graph and replays it as many times as needed, possibly on several threads, without going back to Python between the tasks.

Calls execute the tasks once and bind them; a sequence replays the resulting graph.

Two consequences:

  • the first execution, when the graph is described, comes on top of those of the sequence. To only describe the graph, disable it with spu.Task.call_auto_exec = False or auto_exec=False;
  • in-place operations (+=, forward sockets) are replayed on data that has already been modified (see A sequence replays the graph).

docs.title: Sequences and pipelines
docs.text:
A sequence is built from its first tasks (or from sockets, from which StreamPU finds the first tasks) and contains every task reachable through the bindings. On n threads, the modules are cloned n times and each thread runs its own copy of the graph on its own frames.

A pipeline splits the graph into stages, each stage being a sequence with its own number of threads, connected to the next one by buffers. It allows modules that cannot be cloned (sources, sinks…) to be combined with multithreaded stages.

Spatial parallelism (top) and temporal parallelism (bottom).

See Building a Sequence and Running in parallel.

docs.title: Install for development
docs.text:
Install the package in editable mode with the development dependencies (isort, black, flake8, pytest, pybind11-stubgen, pre-commit) and the documentation dependencies:

pip install -ve '.[dev,docs]'

docs.title: Code formatting and linting
docs.text:
The Python code of streampu/ and examples/ is formatted with isort and black, and checked with flake8. Their settings are in pyproject.toml and .flake8. The CI rejects code that does not pass these checks.

The script scripts/lint.sh runs the three tools:

scripts/lint.sh           # format the code in place, then run flake8
scripts/lint.sh --check   # only check, like the CI

To run these checks automatically on the modified files at each commit, install the pre-commit hooks once:

pre-commit install
pre-commit run --all-files   # optional: check the whole repository

The C++ code of src/ and include/ is formatted with clang-format:

scripts/apply_clang_format.sh

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: pytest --pyargs streampu

docs.title: Type stubs of the C++ bindings
docs.text:
The folder streampu/_ext/ contains the type stubs (.pyi) of the compiled module streampu._ext. They are used by the API reference and by IDEs. Regenerate them each time the C++ bindings change, and commit the result:

scripts/generate_stubs.sh

The CI job stubs checks that they are up to date.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The documentation is written in Markdown in docs/ and built with MkDocs:

mkdocs serve            # local preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict   # same check as the CI

The task graphs of the documentation (docs/assets/*.svg) are drawn with the TikZ library pgflibrarystreampu. Their sources are in docs/assets/Tex_files/; rebuild them with a LaTeX distribution providing latex and dvisvgm:

scripts/build_figures.sh               # all the figures
scripts/build_figures.sh index_graph   # one figure

The outputs shown in the examples are written by hand. scripts/check_tutorial.py runs the examples of the documentation and compares their results with these outputs:

python scripts/check_tutorial.py

docs.title: Create a virtual environment
docs.text:
To install pystreampu in a virtual environment, you can use the following commands: 

python3 -m venv env
source env/bin/activate

docs.title: Install from the sources
docs.text:
Clone the repository 

git clone --recursive https://gitlab.bordeaux-inp.fr/rtajan/pystreampu.git
then install the python interface of StreamPU using pip 
pip install ./pystreampu
If you want more information during compilation, use -v option of the pip command.

Warning

The compilation of streampu may take a long time, depending on your machine. You can set the variable CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL to set the number of parallel jobs used during compilation. For example, to use 4 parallel jobs, you can do: 

export CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=4

docs.title: Install with fine-tuning of C++ flags
docs.text:
To install streampu compiled with custom flags, use the following syntax: 

pip install -Ccmake.define.YOUR_CMAKE_FLAG1=CONTENT1 -Ccmake.define.YOUR_CMAKE_FLAG2=CONTENT2 .
where you can replace YOUR_CMAKE_FLAG1 and YOUR_CMAKE_FLAG2 by the flags you want and set CONTENT1 and CONTENT2 values.

docs.title: Run tests
docs.text: pytest --pyargs streampu

docs.title: Install for development
docs.text:
To install streampu for development, you can use the following command: 

pip install -ve './pystreampu[dev,docs]'

Note

This will install the development dependencies, the testing dependencies, and the documentation dependencies. You can then test the package with pytest and build the documentation using mkdocs command.

docs.title: Writing a module in C++
docs.text:
StreamPU can be extended with modules written in C++. They run at full speed, without the GIL, and can keep a state. This guide builds a module Adder with a task add_one that adds 1 to each element of an array of double, then makes it available in Python.

The complete project is in the folder examples/custom_cpp_module of the repository; the code shown on this page is included from it.

custom_cpp_module/
  src/
    Adder.hpp
    Adder.cpp
    wrapper.cpp
  tests/
    test_custom_cpp_module.py
  CMakeLists.txt

docs.title: Declare the module
docs.text:
The class Adder inherits from spu::module::Stateful. The number of elements of the arrays is given to the constructor, and the actual processing is done by the method add_one:

#ifndef ADDER_HPP_
#define ADDER_HPP_

#include <streampu.hpp>

class Adder : public spu::module::Stateful
{
  protected:
    int n_elmts;

  public:
    Adder(const int n_elmts);
    virtual ~Adder() = default;

    void add_one(const double* input, double* output) const;
};

#endif // ADDER_HPP_

docs.title: Implement the module
docs.text:
The constructor declares the task and its sockets, then the codelet, the function executed by the task:

  1. create_task("add_one") creates the task;
  2. create_socket_in<double> and create_socket_out<double> create its input and output sockets of n_elmts elements, and return their indexes;
  3. create_codelet registers a lambda of type int(spu::module::Module&, spu::runtime::Task&, const size_t). It recovers the module and the data pointers of the sockets, calls add_one and returns a status.
#include "Adder.hpp"

Adder::Adder(const int n_elmts)
  : Stateful()
  , n_elmts(n_elmts)
{
    const std::string name = "Adder";
    this->set_name(name);

    auto& p = this->create_task("add_one");                                                  // Create the task
    size_t ps_input = this->template create_socket_in<double>(p, "input", this->n_elmts);    // Create the input socket
    size_t ps_output = this->template create_socket_out<double>(p, "output", this->n_elmts); // Create the output socket

    // create the codelet
    this->create_codelet(
      p,
      [ps_input, ps_output](spu::module::Module& m, spu::runtime::Task& t, const size_t frame_id) -> int
      {
          // Recover the Module and Sockets in the codelet
          auto& adder = static_cast<Adder&>(m);
          double* input = (double*)(t[ps_input].get_dataptr());
          double* output = (double*)(t[ps_output].get_dataptr());

          // Process the data
          adder.add_one(input, output);
          return spu::runtime::status_t::SUCCESS;
      });
}

// Actual implementation of the task.
void
Adder::add_one(const double* input, double* output) const
{
    for (int i = 0; i < this->n_elmts; i++)
        output[i] = input[i] + 1;
}

docs.title: Wrap the module with pybind11
docs.text:
Only the constructor needs to be wrapped: the tasks and sockets created by the constructor are exposed automatically by streampu.

#include "Adder.hpp"
#include <pybind11/pybind11.h>
#include <streampu.hpp>

namespace py = pybind11;
using namespace py::literals;

// Create a python module using PYBIND11, here our module will be named pyaf
PYBIND11_MODULE(my_module, m)
{
    auto pyspu_stateful = (py::object)py::module_::import("streampu");
    // Each extension linked with the static StreamPU library has its own copy of the
    // allocator settings: enable the automatic allocation of the task sockets here too,
    // as streampu does for its own modules.
    spu::tools::Buffer_allocator::set_task_autoalloc(true);
    m.attr("spu") = pyspu_stateful;
    py::class_<Adder, spu::module::Stateful>(m, "Adder").def(py::init<const int>(), "n_elmts"_a);
}

Two lines of the module initialization are required:

  • py::module_::import("streampu") registers the base class spu::module::Stateful with pybind11 before Adder is declared;
  • spu::tools::Buffer_allocator::set_task_autoalloc(true) enables the automatic allocation of the socket buffers. streampu does it for its own modules, but your extension is linked with its own copy of the static StreamPU library, and therefore with its own copy of this setting. Without it, executing a task fails with "some of the inputs/output sockets are not fed".

docs.title: Build the project
docs.text:
The project must be compiled against the StreamPU and pybind11 versions used by the installed streampu package. streampu.get_cmake_dirs() gives the corresponding CMake directories:

>>> import streampu
>>> streampu.get_cmake_dirs()
'path/to/your/site-packages/pybind11/share/cmake:path/to/your/site-packages/streampu/lib/cmake'

Pass them to CMake through CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH:

cd examples/custom_cpp_module
mkdir build && cd build
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=$(python -c "import streampu; print(streampu.get_cmake_dirs())") cmake ..
make
CMakeLists.txt 
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.6)
cmake_policy(SET CMP0054 NEW)
project (my_module)

# Enable C++11
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

# Link with the "Threads library (required to link with AFF3CT after)
set(CMAKE_THREAD_PREFER_PTHREAD ON)
set(THREADS_PREFER_PTHREAD_FLAG ON)
set(PYBIND11_NEWPYTHON ON)

find_package(pybind11 CONFIG REQUIRED )

find_package(Threads REQUIRED)
find_package(cpptrace REQUIRED)
find_package(streampu REQUIRED)
#find_package(pystreampu REQUIRED)

file(GLOB SOURCES "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src/*.cpp")

#add_subdirectory(${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/pybind11/)
pybind11_add_module(my_module-lib MODULE ${SOURCES})

set_target_properties(my_module-lib PROPERTIES
                      OUTPUT_NAME my_module
                      POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE ON) # set -fpic

target_link_libraries     (my_module-lib PRIVATE spu::spu-static-lib)
target_include_directories(my_module-lib PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/src)
#target_include_directories(my_module-lib PUBLIC /Users/rtajan/Codes/sandbox/pystreampu/include)

docs.title: Use the module
docs.text:
The build creates a Python extension my_module in the build folder. Add this folder to the Python path, either in the script:

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/path/to/build")

or in the environment:

export PYTHONPATH=$PYTHONPATH:/path/to/build

The module is then used like any StreamPU module:

>>> import my_module
>>> import streampu as spu
>>> mdl = my_module.Adder(4)
>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3, 4], dtype=spu.float64)
>>> y = mdl.add_one(x)
>>> y
socket([[2. 3. 4. 5.]], dtype=float64, name=output, task=Adder.add_one)

To distribute such a module as a Python package, see Creating a plugin.

docs.title: Creating a plugin
docs.text: A plugin is a separate Python package that extends streampu, typically with new modules written in C++ (see Writing a module in C++) or in Python. Plugins are discovered automatically when streampu is imported.

docs.title: How plugins are discovered
docs.text:
At import, streampu loads every installed package that declares an entry point in the group streampu.plugins. The loaded objects are stored in the dictionary spu.plugins, indexed by the name of their entry point:

>>> import streampu as spu
>>> spu.plugins
{'my_plugin': <module 'my_plugin' from '...'>}

docs.title: Declare the entry point
docs.text:
In the pyproject.toml of the plugin package, declare the module to load:

[project]
name = "my-plugin"
dependencies = ["streampu"]

[project.entry-points."streampu.plugins"]
my_plugin = "my_plugin"

Once the package is installed (pip install .), its modules are available with:

import streampu as spu

mdl = spu.plugins["my_plugin"].Adder(4)

docs.title: Package a C++ module as a plugin
docs.text:
A C++ plugin is built against the StreamPU and pybind11 versions used by the installed streampu package. Their CMake configuration files are given by:

>>> import streampu
>>> streampu.get_cmake_dirs()
'path/to/site-packages/pybind11/share/cmake:path/to/site-packages/streampu/lib/cmake'

With scikit-build-core, the build backend used by streampu itself, the CMake project of Writing a module in C++ can be packaged by adding streampu to the build requirements and passing these directories to CMake through CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH.

docs.title: Measuring performance
docs.text: This guide shows how to measure the time spent in each task of a sequence and how to report values while the sequence runs.

docs.title: Overall duration
docs.text:
The simplest measure is the wall-clock time of the execution:

import time

start = time.perf_counter()
seq.exec_n_times(1000)
print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1e3:.1f} ms")

docs.title: Statistics per task
docs.text:
Each task can record statistics about its executions. They have to be enabled before the execution, with the stats property of the tasks:

import streampu as spu

src = spu.source_random(8, dtype=spu.int64)
inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
out_data, _ = src.generate()
out = inc.increment(out_data)
seq = spu.Sequence(out)

for task in seq.get_tasks_per_threads()[0]:
    task.stats = True

seq.exec_n_times(1000)
seq.show_stats()

show_stats prints one line per task (columns shortened here):

#        MODULE NAME |         TASK NAME | REP | ORDER |   TIMER ||    CALLS |     TIME |   PERC || ...
# -------------------|-------------------|-----|-------|---------||----------|----------|--------||
#             Source |          generate | yes |     0 |       * ||     1001 |     0.00 |  60.28 || ...
#        Incrementer |         increment | yes |     1 |       * ||     1001 |     0.00 |  39.72 || ...
# -------------------|-------------------|-----|-------|---------||----------|----------|--------||
#              TOTAL |                 * | yes |     * |       * ||     1001 |     0.00 | 100.00 || ...

The full table also gives the throughput and the latency of each task (average, minimum and maximum). Here generate and increment were called 1001 times: once when the graph was described, then 1000 times by the sequence.

The statistics are also available from Python, for each task:

Attribute Meaning task.n_calls number of executions task.total_duration total time spent in the task (s) task.avg_duration, task.min_duration, task.max_duration average, minimum and maximum duration of an execution (s) task.reset() reset the statistics

Note

With a multithreaded sequence, each thread has its own copies of the tasks: enable the statistics on all of them.

for tasks in seq.get_tasks_per_threads():
    for task in tasks:
        task.stats = True

For a pipeline, pipeline.show_stats() prints one table per stage.

Warning

Collecting statistics has a small cost. Disable them when measuring the overall performance.

docs.title: Reporting values with probes
docs.text:
Probes are modules that observe the graph during its execution: the value of a socket, the number of executions, the elapsed time… Each probe fills a column of a reporter, and a terminal displays the reporters.

In the following example, a counter is incremented at each execution of the sequence and its value is reported, together with the execution number and the elapsed time.

import streampu as spu

spu.Task.call_auto_exec = False      # describe the graph without executing it

count = spu.array([0], dtype=spu.int32)
count += 1                           # incremented at each execution

reporter = spu.Reporter_probe("Counter", "A simple example")
prb_exec = spu.Probe_occurrence("Exec.", reporter)
prb_count = spu.probe_value(1, "Count", reporter, spu.int32)
prb_time = spu.Probe_time("Time", reporter)
prb_time.set_col_unit("(s)")

prb_count(count)                     # the value probe reads the socket
prb_exec()                           # the other probes have no input socket:
prb_exec.probe.bind(count)           # bind their task to the graph so that they
prb_time()                           # are part of the sequence
prb_time.probe.bind(count)

spu.Task.call_auto_exec = True

terminal = spu.Terminal_dump([reporter])
seq = spu.Sequence(count)

terminal.legend()
seq.exec_n_times(5, terminal)
terminal.report()

The terminal prints the title of the reporter, the name and unit of each column, then one line per execution.

The appearance of a column is set on its probe: set_col_unit, set_col_prec (precision), set_col_size (width) and set_col_fmtflags, for instance prb.set_col_fmtflags(spu.FormatFlags.fixed).

Available probes:

Probe Reports spu.probe_value(size, name, reporter, dtype) the values of a socket spu.Probe_occurrence(name, reporter) the number of executions spu.Probe_time(name, reporter) the elapsed time spu.Probe_timestamp(name, reporter) a timestamp spu.Probe_throughput(data_size, name, reporter) a throughput spu.Probe_latency(name, reporter) a latency

Their behavior is the one of the corresponding C++ probes, described in the StreamPU documentation.

docs.title: Writing a module in Python
docs.text: When the processing you need is not available as a built-in module, you can write it in Python. A spu.Stateless module holds tasks whose codelet, the function executed by the task, is a Python function. Such a module is used exactly like the built-in ones: its tasks can be called, bound, put in a sequence or a pipeline, and duplicated on several threads.

docs.title: Create the module, its task and its sockets
docs.text:
As an example, we write a module with a task scale that multiplies 8 floats by 2.

import streampu as spu

N = 8

mdl = spu.Stateless()
task = mdl.create_task("scale")
mdl.create_socket_in(task, "x", N, spu.float32)
mdl.create_socket_out(task, "y", N, spu.float32)
  • create_task(name) adds a task to the module and returns it;
  • create_socket_in, create_socket_out and create_socket_fwd add an input, output or forward socket to a task, given its name, its number of elements and its data type.

docs.title: Write the codelet
docs.text:
The codelet receives the module, the task and a frame index, and returns a status (0 means success). Inside the codelet, the data of the sockets is accessed without copy through their numpy attribute:

def scale(module, task, frame_id):
    x = task.x.numpy   # or task["x"].numpy
    y = task.y.numpy
    y[:] = 2 * x       # write the output in place
    return 0

mdl.create_codelet(task, scale)

Warning

The output must be written in place (y[:] = ...). Writing y = 2 * x would only rebind the local variable y and leave the socket unchanged.

The arrays are 2D (one row per frame): write the codelet so that it works on all the rows, as above.

docs.title: Use the module
docs.text:
The task can now be called like any other task:

>>> x = spu.arange(0, 8, dtype=spu.float32)
>>> y = mdl.scale(x)
>>> y.numpy
array([[ 0.,  2.,  4.,  6.,  8., 10., 12., 14.]], dtype=float32)

It can be combined with operators and other modules, and replayed by a sequence:

>>> z = mdl.scale(x) + 1
>>> seq = spu.Sequence(z)
>>> seq.exec_n_times(10)

Use spu.help(mdl) to display its tasks and sockets.

docs.title: Several threads
docs.text:
A Stateless module is cloned automatically when it is part of a multithreaded sequence. All the clones share the same codelet function, so the codelet must not keep any state between two calls (in global variables or in a closure): everything it needs must come from its input sockets.

With a regular Python interpreter, the codelets of the different threads cannot run Python code at the same time because of the GIL. Two solutions:

  • compile the heavy part of the codelet with numba and the nogil=True option, so that the compiled code runs without holding the GIL:

    import numba

@numba.njit(nogil=True, cache=True)
def _scale(x, y):
    for f in range(x.shape[0]):
        for i in range(x.shape[1]):
            y[f, i] = 2 * x[f, i]

def scale(module, task, frame_id):
    _scale(task.x.numpy, task.y.numpy)
    return 0

  • use a free-threaded Python (3.14t) and run it with PYTHON_GIL=0: the codelets of all the threads then run in parallel.

The scripts of examples/custom_python_module compare the execution times of a Python module with different Python interpreters and numbers of threads.

docs.title: Modules with a state
docs.text:
A Stateless module cannot hold parameters or data of its own. When the processing depends on parameters or must keep data between two executions, derive a class from Stateful_core. The example below keeps one sample out of F; F is the state of the module:

"""Minimal example of a module written in Python with a state: keep one sample out of F."""

import streampu as spu
from streampu._ext.sfl import Stateful_core


class Downsampler(Stateful_core):
    """Stateful module with one task, `downsample`, that keeps one sample out of `F`.

    The parameter `F` is stored as a Python attribute of the module: it is its state.
    """

    def __init__(self, N, F=1, dtype=spu.float32):
        super().__init__()
        self.F = F

        task = self.create_task("downsample")
        self.create_socket_in(task, "input", N, dtype)
        self.create_socket_out(task, "output", N // F, dtype)
        self.create_codelet(task, Downsampler._downsample)

    @staticmethod
    def _downsample(mdl, tsk, frame_id):
        # `mdl` is the module that executes the task: the original one or one of its clones.
        # Always read the state from `mdl`, never from a `self` captured when the codelet was created.
        out = tsk["output"].numpy
        out[:] = tsk["input"].numpy[:, : out.shape[1] * mdl.F : mdl.F]
        return 0

    def clone(self):
        # Called by StreamPU to duplicate the module on several threads. Only the Python state
        # is copied here: the tasks, sockets and codelets are copied by StreamPU itself, so
        # `__init__` must not be called again. `type(self)` keeps the class of subclasses.
        other = type(self).__new__(type(self))
        Stateful_core.__init__(other)
        other.F = self.F
        return other

It is used like any other module:

>>> from downsampler import Downsampler
>>> dwn = Downsampler(N=8, F=2, dtype=spu.int32)
>>> y = dwn.downsample(spu.array(list(range(8)), dtype=spu.int32))
>>> y.numpy
array([[0, 2, 4, 6]], dtype=int32)

Three rules make such a module work on several threads:

  1. Store the state as attributes of the module (self.F).
  2. Read the state from the mdl argument of the codelet, never from a self captured when the codelet is created: the same codelet is executed by every clone of the module, and mdl is the clone that executes it.
  3. Implement clone(). StreamPU calls it to duplicate the module, then copies the tasks, sockets and codelets itself. clone() must therefore create an instance of the same class, type(self), without calling __init__ (which would create the tasks a second time), and only copy the Python state.

Note

Stateful_core is imported from streampu._ext.sfl: this part of the API may still evolve.

The script examples/custom_python_module/custom_python_module.py uses this module in a multithreaded sequence and measures its duration for different numbers of threads.

docs.title: Performance with several threads
docs.text:
The script examples/custom_python_module/custom_python_module.py runs 10,000 executions of a sequence containing the Downsampler above, for 1 to 16 threads, with different Python interpreters. As a reference, it also runs the same processing with C++ modules (a relayer followed by a slice x[::4]).

Duration of 10,000 executions of a sequence with a Python module or with C++ modules, for 1 to 16 threads. Configuration 1 thread 16 threads Python 3.12, GIL 35 ms 142 ms Python 3.14t, no GIL (PYTHON_GIL=0) 39 ms 164 ms Python 3.14t, GIL (PYTHON_GIL=1) 39 ms 932 ms C++ modules 13.9 ms 1.4 ms

What it shows (note the logarithmic scale):

  • The C++ modules are faster and scale with the number of threads: on 1 thread, they are 2.5 times faster than the Python module; on 16 threads, they run 10 times faster than on 1 thread, and about 100 times faster than the best Python configuration.
  • The Python module does not scale: the work done by its codelet is tiny (a NumPy slice), so the cost of entering the Python interpreter at each call dominates, and adding threads only adds contention. With the GIL, the threads wait for each other and the duration increases with the number of threads; on Python 3.14t with the GIL enabled, this is particularly costly.
  • Without the GIL (Python 3.14t, PYTHON_GIL=0), the duration stays flat up to 3 threads and grows slowly afterwards, but never decreases.

To benefit from several threads with a Python module, give each call more work (larger frames, several frames per execution with n_frames), release the GIL in the heavy part of the codelet (numba with nogil=True), or write the module in C++.

Run examples/custom_python_module/perform_comparison.sh to reproduce these measures on your machine.

docs.title: When to write a C++ module instead
docs.text: A Python codelet is convenient but each call has a cost. For processing that is executed very often on small data, write the module in C++: see Writing a module in C++.

docs.title: Working with sockets
docs.text:
Sockets can be combined with the usual Python operators. Each operation creates a small StreamPU module (adder, comparator, reducer…), binds it to its operands and executes it. The result is a new socket that can be used in turn, so that a whole computation can be written as plain Python expressions and then replayed by a Sequence.

>>> import streampu as spu

docs.title: Create sockets
docs.text:
Function Result spu.array(data, dtype=None) socket holding data (list, scalar or NumPy array) spu.zeros(n, dtype=spu.float32) n zeros spu.ones(n, dtype=spu.float32) n ones spu.arange(start, stop, step=1, dtype=spu.float32) evenly spaced values, like np.arange 
>>> spu.array([1, 2, 3])
socket([[1 2 3]], dtype=int64, name=data, task=Array.read)
>>> spu.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=spu.float32)
socket([[1. 2. 3.]], dtype=float32, name=data, task=Array.read)

All these functions also accept an n_frames argument to replicate the data on several frames.

Note

The available data types are spu.int8, spu.int16, spu.int32, spu.int64, spu.uint8, spu.uint16, spu.uint32, spu.uint64, spu.float32 and spu.float64. Without dtype, spu.array keeps the NumPy type of the data.

Warning

spu.array is designed for 1D data. A 2D list is interpreted as one row per frame.

docs.title: Arithmetic operators
docs.text:
+, -, * and / work between two sockets of the same size, or between a socket and a scalar, on either side:

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3])
>>> (x + 1).numpy
array([[2, 3, 4]], dtype=int64)
>>> (10 - x).numpy
array([[9, 8, 7]], dtype=int64)
>>> (x * x).numpy
array([[1, 4, 9]], dtype=int64)

The result has the data type of the first socket, and the other operand is converted to this type. As a consequence, dividing integer sockets performs an integer division:

>>> x = spu.array([12, 7], dtype=spu.int32)
>>> (x / 2).numpy
array([[6, 3]], dtype=int32)
>>> (x.astype(spu.float32) / 2).numpy
array([[6. , 3.5]], dtype=float32)

Each operator also exists as a function, which accepts an output_dtype argument: spu.add, spu.sub, spu.mul and spu.div.

docs.title: In-place operators
docs.text:
+=, -=, *=, /=, &=, |= and ^= modify the data of the socket itself instead of creating a new socket:

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3])
>>> x += 1
>>> x *= 2
>>> x.numpy
array([[4, 6, 8]], dtype=int64)

Warning

In-place operations are replayed by a sequence on data that has already been modified. See A sequence replays the graph.

docs.title: Comparisons
docs.text:
==, !=, <, <=, > and >= return a socket of 0 and 1, with the data type of the first operand:

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3])
>>> (x > 1).numpy
array([[0, 1, 1]], dtype=int64)
>>> (x == 2).numpy
array([[0, 1, 0]], dtype=int64)

Function forms: spu.equal, spu.not_equal, spu.less, spu.less_equal, spu.greater, spu.greater_equal.

docs.title: Bitwise operators
docs.text:
&, |, ^ and ~ work on integer sockets (functions spu.bitwise_and, spu.bitwise_or, spu.bitwise_xor and spu.bitwise_not):

>>> x = spu.array([12], dtype=spu.int32)
>>> (~x).numpy
array([[-13]], dtype=int32)

docs.title: Unary operations
docs.text:
Operation Function -x spu.neg(x) abs(x) spu.abs(x) ~x spu.bitwise_not(x) x.astype(dtype) spu.cast(x, dtype) 
>>> x = spu.array([12], dtype=spu.int32)
>>> (-x).numpy
array([[-12]], dtype=int32)
>>> x.astype(spu.float32).numpy
array([[12.]], dtype=float32)

docs.title: Reductions, minimum and maximum
docs.text:
spu.sum, spu.prod, spu.min, spu.max, spu.all and spu.any reduce a socket to a single value:

>>> x = spu.array([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
>>> spu.sum(x).numpy
array([[14]], dtype=int64)
>>> spu.max(x).numpy
array([[5]], dtype=int64)

Given several sockets, spu.min and spu.max compute the element-wise minimum or maximum:

>>> y = spu.array([2, 7, 1, 8, 2])
>>> spu.min(x, y).numpy
array([[2, 1, 1, 1, 2]], dtype=int64)

docs.title: Slicing
docs.text:
Sockets support reading and writing with an index, a slice or a list of indices:

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
>>> x[1:4].numpy
array([[2, 3, 4]], dtype=int64)
>>> x[::2] = [10, 30, 50]
>>> x.numpy
array([[10,  2, 30,  4, 50]], dtype=int64)

Reading and writing can be combined, for instance to transform every other element:

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
>>> x[::2] = 2 * x[::2] + 1
>>> x.numpy
array([[ 3,  2,  7,  4, 11]], dtype=int64)

docs.title: Mixing operators and modules
docs.text:
The sockets produced by operators are regular sockets: they can be given to any task, and the outputs of any task can be used with operators.

>>> src = spu.source_random(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> out_data, _ = src.generate()
>>> y = 2 * inc.increment(out_data) - 1
>>> seq = spu.Sequence(y)
>>> seq.exec_seq()

Here y is computed from fresh random bits at each execution of seq.

docs.title: Visualizing a graph
docs.text: When a graph grows, it becomes hard to check from the code how its tasks are bound. A sequence (or a pipeline) can export its graph in the Graphviz DOT format.

docs.title: Export the graph
docs.text:
import streampu as spu

src = spu.source_random(8, dtype=spu.int64)
inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
out_data, _ = src.generate()
out = inc.increment(out_data)

seq = spu.Sequence(out)
seq.export_dot("seq.dot")

spu.Pipeline provides the same export_dot method.

docs.title: Render it
docs.text:
With Graphviz installed, convert the file into an image:

dot -Tsvg seq.dot -o seq.svg

or from Python, with the graphviz package:

import graphviz

graphviz.Source.from_file("seq.dot").render("seq", format="svg")

docs.title: Read the figure
docs.text:
The DOT file describes nested boxes:

  • the outer boxes are the sub-sequences of the sequence (a sequence is split into sub-sequences when it contains control flow, such as switches or loops);
  • inside, each box is a module, labelled with its name and its execution order (exec order);
  • inside a module, each box is a task, labelled with its name and its id;
  • inside a task, each node is a socket, labelled with its direction, its index and its name: in[0]:in, out[1]:out, fwd[0]:data…;
  • the arrows are the bindings between sockets.

Reading the execution order of the modules is a good way to check that a graph runs the tasks in the expected order.

A processing step of a module: the code executed by a node of the data-flow graph.

docs.title: First steps with StreamPU in Python
docs.text:
This section presents the first steps for playing with StreamPU in Python. It covers the following key concepts of StreamPU:

  • socket: the data holder
  • task: the data processing
  • module: the tasks holder
  • sequence: a directed and acyclic graph of tasks

docs.title: How to import StreamPU?
docs.text:
As every Python package StreamPU may be imported using the import interface.

>>> import streampu as spu

docs.title: Organisation of this documentation
docs.text:
Code blocks starting with >>> are typed in a Python interpreter; the lines without prompt are the output. The following code block is the start of an example running through this page. 

>>> x = spu.array([1,2,3,4])

>>> x
socket([[1 2 3 4]], dtype=int64, name=data, task=Array.read)

As the output suggests, x is a Socket.

docs.title: What is a Socket ?
docs.text:
A socket is a way to exchange data between tasks (that process this data). The output of the previous example 

socket([[1 2 3 4]], dtype=int64, name=data, task=Array.read)
indicates that sockets have the following attributes:

  • name: the name of the socket in the task
  • dtype : data type
  • task : the task that holds this socket

docs.title: The name of a socket
docs.text:
You may get the name of a socket as follows 

>>> x.name
'data'

Warning

The name attribute of a socket is read-only, you cannot change it.

The name of a socket will be important when you will want to bind the output of a task to the input of another task.

docs.title: Get the task that owns a socket
docs.text:
To recover the task that holds a socket just do 

>>> x.task
<streampu._ext.core.Task object at 0x10618c3f0>

Warning

  1. The task attribute of a socket is read-only, you cannot change it.
  2. streampu._ext indicates that the Task class belongs to the C++ part of streampu package.

docs.title: Get the socket data type (dtype)
docs.text:
The data stored in a socket is strongly typed: 

>>> x.dtype
spu.int64
This output indicates that the elements of x are integers stored on 64 bits.

StreamPU data types

spu recognizes the following data types:

  • Unsigned integers: spu.uint8, spu.uint16, spu.uint32, spu.uint64
  • Signed integers: spu.int8, spu.int16, spu.int32, spu.int64
  • Floating point: spu.float32, spu.float64

docs.title: Accessing the socket direction
docs.text:
In addition to its name, task and dtype attributes, another important concept is the socket direction. There are 3 different types of socket directions:

  • Input socket: read only data,
  • Output socket: write only data,
  • Forward socket: read and write data.

The socket direction can be recovered as follows 

>>> x.direction
<directions.FWD: 2>
Here x is a forward socket.

Socket directions

Socket directions are stored in the enum spu.Socket.directions:

  • spu.Socket.directions.IN: input socket
  • spu.Socket.directions.OUT: output socket
  • spu.Socket.directions.FWD: forward socket

docs.title: Creating a socket from data
docs.text:
As we have seen in the example, the function spu.array converts the list [1,2,3,4] into a socket.

The same goes for a 1D NumPy array.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> x = np.array([1,2,3,4], dtype = np.int8)
>>> x
array([1, 2, 3, 4], dtype=int8)
>>> y = spu.array(x)
>>> y
socket([[1 2 3 4]], dtype=int8, name=data, task=Array.read)
From this example, you can see that the NumPy dtype int8 is propagated to the socket created by spu.array.

Warning

There is no copy when creating a socket from a NumPy array! Hence, if we modify the numpy data, the socket data is modified accordingly, for example 

>>> x[2] = 42
>>> y
socket([[ 1  2 42  4]], dtype=int8, name=data, task=Array.read)

docs.title: Converting a socket into a numpy array
docs.text:
You can create a NumPy array from a socket by using its numpy attribute as follows 

>>> x = spu.array([1,2,3,4])
>>> y = x.numpy
>>> y
array([[1, 2, 3, 4]], dtype=int64)

Note

  1. The NumPy array will have the numpy dtype corresponding to the one of the socket.
  2. This conversion is also copy-free, hence in the previous example, changing y will affect the data of x.

docs.title: What is a module?
docs.text:
A module is an object that can store one or several tasks.

For example, suppose that we want to randomly generate 8 bits from a Bernoulli distribution. We can build this module from the factory method spu.source_random as follows

>>> src = spu.source_random(8, dtype = spu.int64)
>>> src
<streampu._ext.src.Source_random_int64 object at 0x106f82150>

Note

In this example, the type of src is Source_random_int64. Within the package, this class is located in: streampu._ext.src.

Source_random_int64 indicates that the output dtype of the data generated by src will have int64 dtype.

docs.title: How to know the tasks of a given module?
docs.text:
There are several ways of accessing the tasks of a module. The simpler one is by accessing its tasks attribute to get the list of all the module's tasks as shown in the following example. 

>>> src.tasks
[<streampu._ext.core.Task object at 0x1065c0970>]

If you just want to get information about the tasks of one module, spu comes with spu.help

>>> spu.help(src)
# module:
# |- name: Source_random
# |- short name: Source
# |- n_frames: 1
# |- tasks:
# |  |- name: generate
# |  |  |- sockets out:
# |  |  |  |- out_data: { n_elts = 8, datatype = int64 }
# |  |  |  |- out_count: { n_elts = 1, datatype = uint32 }
# |  |  |  |- status: { n_elts = 1, datatype = int32 }

Here we see that src has one task named generate that has 3 outputs:

  • out_data: 8 elements of type int64
  • out_count: 1 element of type uint32
  • status: 1 element of type int32

docs.title: What is a task?
docs.text: According to the StreamPU documentation, "a task represents the code executed by a node in the data flow graph".

docs.title: Accessing the task of a module
Using the tasks attribute
docs.text:
There are several ways of getting the task of a given module.

The first one is by using the tasks attribute as follows 

>>> src.tasks[0]
<streampu._ext.core.Task object at 0x1065c0970>

docs.title: Using mdl[tsk_name]
docs.text:
If you know the name of the task, you can also write 

>>> src['generate']
<streampu._ext.core.Task object at 0x1065c0970>

docs.title: Using mdl.tsk_name
docs.text:
A task can also be accessed as if it is a module attribute as follows 

>>> src.generate
<streampu._ext.core.Task object at 0x1065c0970>

Note

All methods to access a task will get the same object. The three methods are kept so that a C++ user of StreamPU can easily translate a C++ program to a python program.

docs.title: How to know the sockets of a task
docs.text:
To know the sockets of a task, we can simply use spu.help, but on a task. 

>>> spu.help(src.generate)
|- name: generate
|  |- sockets out:
|  |  |- out_data: { n_elts = 8, datatype = int64 }
|  |  |- out_count: { n_elts = 1, datatype = uint32 }
|  |  |- status: { n_elts = 1, datatype = int32 }

docs.title: How to access a socket of a task?
Using the sockets attribute of a task
docs.text:
Every task has a sockets attribute that contains the lists of its sockets.

Warning

The sockets in tsk.sockets appear in the order of their creation. There is no convention for having for example the input sockets first.

Use tsk.inputs, tsk.outputs, and tsk.forwards to get the inputs, output or forward sockets respectively.

docs.title: By getting the socket_name item of a socket
docs.text:
We can access a socket of a task as follows 

>>> tsk = src['generate']
>>> tsk['out_data']
socket([[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]], dtype=int64, name=out_data, task=Source_random.generate)

docs.title: By getting the task_name::socket_name item of a module
docs.text:
Another way of accessing the same socket is by accessing the item 'task_name::socket_name' of a module as in the following example. 

>>> src['generate::out_data']
socket([[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]], dtype=int64, name=out_data, task=Source_random.generate)

docs.title: By getting the socket_name attribute of a task
docs.text:
The last way for accessing the same socket is by using the socket name as a task attribute as follows. 

>>> src.generate.out_data
socket([[0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0]], dtype=int64, name=out_data, task=Source_random.generate)

Note

Whatever the way you used to access the socket out_data in the previous examples, the content of the socket is filled with 0. This is due to the fact that the task has never been executed.

docs.title: Execute a Task
docs.text:
The sockets of a task are filled when the task is executed. Let us execute the task generate of src. 

>>> src['generate'].exec()
>>> src.generate.out_data
socket([[0 1 1 0 1 1 1 1]], dtype=int64, name=out_data, task=Source_random.generate)
The generated bits are now written inside the socket data.

docs.title: How to build a processing sequence?
docs.text:
Suppose that we now want to increment the bits of out_data. To do so, we start by building an incrementer (which is also a module).

>>> inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
We can remark that inc has a task called increment that has one input socket called in and one output socket called out.

Warning

As in is a keyword of the python language, we cannot use the syntax inc.increment.in to access it. 

>>> inc.increment.in
File "<stdin>", line 1
    inc.increment.in
                ^^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax
Use the item syntax instead: inc['increment::in'] or inc.increment['in'].

docs.title: Socket binding
docs.text:
To link the source src and the incrementer inc, the output socket out_data of the task generate of the module src should be "bound" to the input socket in of the task increment of the module inc.

inc['increment::in'] = src['generate::out_data']

This line is schematically equivalent to the following figure.

Figure: Binding between src.generate.out_data and inc.increment.in.

docs.title: Tasks execution
docs.text:
Now we can execute the tasks of each module.

>>> src['generate'].exec()
>>> src['generate::out_data']
socket([[1 0 0 1 1 0 1 0]], dtype=int64, name=out_data, task=Source_random.generate)
>>> inc['increment'].exec()
>>> inc['increment::out']
socket([[2 1 1 2 2 1 2 1]], dtype=int64, name=out, task=Incrementer.increment)

The values are random: yours will differ, but each output of increment is the corresponding output of generate plus one.

docs.title: Debug mode activation
docs.text:
You can see that the data is automatically transferred from the output of generate to the input of increment. The data printing can also be handled automatically by setting the debug property of the tasks to True.

>>> src['generate'].debug = True
>>> inc['increment'].debug = True
>>> src['generate'].exec()
# Source_random::generate(int64 out_data[8], uint32 out_count[1])
# {OUT} out_data  = [    0,     0,     0,     1,     0,     1,     1,     0]
# {OUT} out_count = [    8]
# Returned status: [0 'SUCCESS']
#
>>> inc['increment'].exec()
# Incrementer::increment(const int64 in[8], int64 out[8])
# {IN}  in  = [    0,     0,     0,     1,     0,     1,     1,     0]
# {OUT} out = [    1,     1,     1,     2,     1,     2,     2,     1]
# Returned status: [0 'SUCCESS']
#
>>>

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: The next pages show how to simplify these steps and how to replay the graph with a Sequence.

docs.title: Going further with StreamPU in Python
docs.text: Now that you are familiar with the basic concepts of StreamPU, including the module, task, and socket abstractions, we will show how the previous steps can be simplified.

docs.title: Build the modules
docs.text:
We keep the same example: suppose that we want to randomly generate 8 bits from a Bernoulli distribution and increment these bits. As we have seen in the previous steps, we can build the modules as follows: 

>>> src = spu.source_random(8, dtype = spu.int64)
>>> src.generate.debug = True
>>> inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> inc.increment.debug = True

In the previous steps, we have seen how to connect the modules and execute the graph. However, we can simplify this process by "calling" a task directly as a method of the module. Calling a task binds its sockets and executes it.

docs.title: Using a task as a method of the module
docs.text:
Schematically, we can call a task with 2 input sockets and 3 forward sockets as a method of the module as follows: 

>>> outputs = module.task(s0, s1, sf0, sf1, sf2)
where

  • s0 and s1 are output or forward sockets of another module that will be bound to the two input sockets of module.task
  • sf0, sf1, and sf2 are three output or forward sockets bound to the corresponding forward sockets of module.task.
  • outputs is a tuple of the output sockets of module.task (or a single socket if the task has only one output socket).

The arguments are bound to the input and forward sockets in the order of their creation, i.e. the order of task.sockets once the output sockets are removed. Use spu.help(module.task) to check this order.

Back to our first example, we want to call the increment with the output named out_data of the src module as input. Let's see how to do this. First we need to get the output socket of the src module. 

>>> out_data = src.generate['out_data']
Then, we can call the increment task as a method of the inc module as follows: 
>>> inc["increment::in"]
socket([], dtype=int64, name=in, task=Incrementer.increment)
>>> out = inc.increment(out_data)
# Incrementer::increment(const int64 in[8], int64 out[8])
# {IN}  in  = [    0,     0,     0,     0,     0,     0,     0,     0]
# {OUT} out = [    1,     1,     1,     1,     1,     1,     1,     1]
# Returned status: [0 'SUCCESS']
As we can see in the above example, the input socket increment::in is empty at the beginning. This is because this socket is dangling and not connected to any output socket. After calling inc.increment, the input socket is automatically bound to the output socket src.generate['out_data'] (named out_data in the example). After this step, both sockets share the same data. Since src.generate has not been executed yet, the output socket out_data is still filled with 0. However, calling inc.increment has also executed the task increment, indeed out is filled with 1.

To check that the binding step has been done correctly, we can execute both tasks again as in the first steps. 

>>> src.generate.exec()
# Source_random::generate(int64 out_data[8], uint32 out_count[1])
# {OUT} out_data  = [    0,     1,     1,     0,     1,     1,     1,     1]
# {OUT} out_count = [    8]
# Returned status: [0 'SUCCESS']
>>> inc.increment.exec()
# Incrementer::increment(const int64 in[8], int64 out[8])
# {IN}  in  = [    0,     1,     1,     0,     1,     1,     1,     1]
# {OUT} out = [    1,     2,     2,     1,     2,     2,     2,     2]
# Returned status: [0 'SUCCESS']
This time, the output of the src.generate task is filled with random bits and the output of the inc.increment task is filled with the incremented values.

docs.title: Binding sockets by name
docs.text:
Sockets can also be bound with keyword arguments named after the sockets of the task. This is the only way to call a task with a socket named after a Python keyword, such as in: 

>>> out = inc.increment(**{"in": out_data})

docs.title: Binding without executing
docs.text:
By default, calling a task executes it. To only bind the sockets, pass auto_exec=False: 

>>> out = inc.increment(out_data, auto_exec=False)
You can also disable the automatic execution for every call by setting spu.Task.call_auto_exec = False, which is convenient when you only want to describe a graph that will be executed later by a Sequence.

docs.title: Calling a task with no input sockets
docs.text:
In the previous example, we have seen how to call a task with input sockets. However, we can also call a task with no input sockets. In this case, we can simply call the task as a method of the module without any arguments. For example, if we want to call the generate task of the src module, we can do it as follows: 

>>> out_data, out_count = src.generate()
As generate has two output sockets (besides status), the call returns a tuple.

Note

The main difference between 

>>> out_data = src.generate['out_data']
and 
>>> out_data, _ = src.generate()
is that the first one retrieves a specific output socket from the task, while the second one executes the task before returning its output sockets.

Warning

When calling a task, the output socket named status is not returned despite always being an output socket of the task. You can retrieve the status as follows: 

>>> src.generate.status
socket([[0]], dtype=int32, name=status, task=Source_random.generate)

docs.title: Comparing the two approaches
docs.text:
In the previous steps, we have seen two different approaches to build and execute this simple graph. The first approach is to build the modules, connect the sockets, and then execute the tasks as shown in the following code example. 

>>> src = spu.source_random(8, dtype = spu.int64)
>>> inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> inc['increment::in'] = src['generate::out_data']
>>> src['generate'].exec()
>>> inc['increment'].exec()

The second approach is to call the tasks as methods of the modules. 

>>> src = spu.source_random(8, dtype = spu.int64)
>>> inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> out_data = src.generate()[0]
>>> out = inc.increment(out_data)
Both approaches are valid and can be used depending on the situation.

In both cases, the tasks are bound together into a graph. The next page shows how to capture this graph in a Sequence and execute it many times.

docs.title: Running in parallel
docs.text:
StreamPU extracts two kinds of parallelism from a streaming application (Cassagne et al., 2023):

  • spatial parallelism: the whole sequence is duplicated on several threads, each thread processing its own frames;
  • temporal parallelism: the graph is split into a pipeline of stages that run concurrently, like an assembly line.

Both are available from Python. The execution itself happens in C++ and the Python GIL is released while a sequence or a pipeline runs.

docs.title: Duplicating a sequence on several threads
Describe the graph
docs.text:
We build a chain of six incrementers between an initializer (which outputs constant data) and a finalizer (which keeps the last data it received). Each incrementer sleeps 5 µs per execution (ns=5000) to simulate some work.

import time
import streampu as spu

data_length = 2048
n_threads = 4

initializer = spu.initializer(data_length, dtype=spu.uint8)
incs = [spu.incrementer(data_length, ns=5000, dtype=spu.uint8) for _ in range(6)]
finalizer = spu.finalizer(data_length, dtype=spu.uint8)

x = initializer.initialize()
y = x
for inc in incs:
    y = inc.increment(y)
finalizer.finalize(y)

docs.title: Build a multithreaded sequence
docs.text:
The second argument of spu.Sequence is the number of threads:

seq = spu.Sequence(x.task, n_threads)

When n_threads > 1, StreamPU clones every module of the graph so that each thread works on its own copy. All the built-in modules used here can be cloned, as well as the Stateless modules written in Python.

Warning

Some modules cannot be cloned, typically sources and sinks that read or write a file (source_user_binary, sink_user_binary…). They cannot be part of a multithreaded sequence: use a pipeline to keep them on a single thread.

docs.title: Work with the clones
docs.text:
The modules you created are the ones of the first thread. To reach the copies used by every thread, use get_cloned_modules. Here, each thread gets different initial data:

for tid, ini in enumerate(seq.get_cloned_modules(initializer)):
    ini.data_init[0][:] = tid   # first (and only) frame of this thread

Then run the sequence and measure its duration:

start = time.perf_counter()
seq.exec_n_times(1000)
print(f"Elapsed: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f} s")

for tid, fin in enumerate(seq.get_cloned_modules(finalizer)):
    print(tid, fin.final_data[0][:4])   # each thread outputs tid + 6

The chain sleeps 6 × 5 µs per execution, so 1000 executions take about 30 ms on one thread. With 4 threads, it ideally drops to 30 / 4 ≈ 7.5 ms. Try different values of n_threads to see how the duration evolves on your machine (spu._ext.get_hardware_concurrency() gives the number of hardware threads).

docs.title: Useful options
docs.text: Option Effect seq.n_frames = 4 each execution processes 4 frames per thread seq.no_copy_mode = True avoid data copies between tasks when possible spu.Sequence(..., thread_pinning=True) pin each thread to a core

docs.title: Splitting the graph into a pipeline
docs.text: A pipeline cuts the graph into stages. Each stage is a sequence running on its own thread(s), and consecutive stages exchange frames through synchronization buffers. This is the way to combine non-clonable modules (sources, sinks…) with a multithreaded processing.

docs.title: Describe the graph
docs.text:
This time the data is read from a file by source_user_binary, goes through six relayer modules (which copy their input to their output after a short sleep), and is written to another file by sink_user_binary.

import os
import streampu as spu

spu.Signal_handler.init()

data_length = 2048
n_threads = 4

with open("file.in", "wb") as f:          # some data to process
    f.write(os.urandom(data_length * 100))

source = spu.source_user_binary(data_length, "file.in", auto_reset=False, dtype=spu.uint8)
sink = spu.sink_user_binary(data_length, "file.out", dtype=spu.uint8)
rlys = [spu.relayer(data_length, ns=5000, dtype=spu.uint8) for _ in range(6)]

spu.Task.call_auto_exec = False   # describe the graph without executing it
data, count = source.generate()
for rly in rlys:
    data = rly.relay(data)
sink.send_count(data, count)
spu.Task.call_auto_exec = True

Note

Here, the automatic execution of the tasks is disabled while the graph is described. Otherwise, calling source.generate() would already consume the first frame of the file.

docs.title: Build and run the pipeline
docs.text:
pipeline = spu.Pipeline(
    [source.generate],    # first tasks of the graph
    [sink.send_count],    # last tasks of the graph
    [                     # stages: [first tasks, last tasks, excluded tasks]
        [[source.generate], [source.generate], []],
        [[rlys[0].relay], [rlys[-1].relay], []],
        [[sink.send_count], [sink.send_count], []],
    ],
    [1, n_threads, 1],    # number of threads per stage
    [16, 16],             # size of the buffers between consecutive stages
    [False, False],       # active waiting between stages
)
pipeline.exec()

The pipeline has three stages: the source on one thread, the six relayers duplicated on n_threads threads, and the sink on one thread. pipeline.exec() returns when the source reaches the end of the file (auto_reset=False). The output file is then identical to the input file.

Like a sequence, a pipeline offers n_frames, export_dot(...), show_stats() and get_modules(...). Its stages property gives access to the sequence of each stage.

docs.title: Python modules and the GIL
docs.text: The built-in modules are written in C++ and run in parallel without any restriction. Modules written in Python (see Writing a module in Python) execute Python code in each thread: with a regular Python interpreter, the GIL lets only one of them run at a time. With a free-threaded Python (3.14t, run with PYTHON_GIL=0), they can run truly in parallel. The example examples/custom_python_module compares these configurations.

docs.title: Building and running a Sequence
docs.text: In the previous pages, tasks were executed one by one, by hand. This is perfect to explore StreamPU but a streaming application runs the same processing over and over. A Sequence captures the graph of bound tasks and replays it as many times as needed, on one or several threads.

docs.title: Describe the graph
docs.text:
We keep the example of the previous pages: a source generates 8 random bits and an incrementer adds one to each of them.

>>> import streampu as spu
>>> src = spu.source_random(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> inc = spu.incrementer(8, dtype=spu.int64)
>>> out_data, _ = src.generate()
>>> out = inc.increment(out_data)

Remember that calling a task does two things: it binds its sockets to the given sockets and it executes the task once. After these lines, src.generate and inc.increment are bound together: they form a graph.

Tip

If you only want to describe the graph, without executing anything, set spu.Task.call_auto_exec = False before calling the tasks, or pass auto_exec=False to each call (see Going further).

docs.title: Build the Sequence
docs.text:
The simplest way to build a sequence is to give it the socket(s) you are interested in:

>>> seq = spu.Sequence(out)

From out, StreamPU walks the bindings backwards until it finds the first tasks of the graph (tasks without input sockets, such as src.generate). The sequence then contains every task reachable from these first tasks.

Other ways to build a sequence:

Call Meaning spu.Sequence(out) graph leading to the socket out spu.Sequence([s1, s2]) graph leading to several sockets spu.Sequence(src.generate) graph starting from the task src.generate spu.Sequence(first_task, last_task) part of the graph between two tasks

You can check the boundaries of a sequence with its first_tasks and last_tasks properties. They hold one list of tasks per thread:

>>> [t.name for t in seq.first_tasks[0]]
['generate']
>>> [t.name for t in seq.last_tasks[0]]
['increment']

docs.title: Execute the Sequence
docs.text:
A sequence offers several ways of being executed:

Method Behavior seq.exec_seq() executes the whole graph once seq.exec_n_times(n) executes the graph n times seq.exec() executes the graph until a module says it is done (for instance a source that reached the end of its file) seq.exec_step(tid) executes the next task only, for step-by-step debugging

Let's run our sequence once and look at the sockets:

>>> seq.exec_seq()
>>> out_data
socket([[0 1 1 0 0 1 0 1]], dtype=int64, name=out_data, task=Source_random.generate)
>>> out
socket([[1 2 2 1 1 2 1 2]], dtype=int64, name=out, task=Incrementer.increment)

Each execution generates new random bits, and out always holds out_data plus one.

To follow what happens during several executions, enable the debug mode of the tasks (see First steps):

>>> src.generate.debug = True
>>> inc.increment.debug = True
>>> seq.exec_n_times(3)

Each task now prints its sockets at each of the 3 executions.

Warning

seq.exec() has no stop condition of its own. With a source that never ends, such as source_random, it runs forever. Call spu.Signal_handler.init() beforehand so that Ctrl+C stops the execution cleanly.

docs.title: A sequence replays the graph
docs.text:
A sequence replays the tasks on the current content of the sockets. Most of the time this is what you want, but be careful with in-place operators (+=, *=, …): they modify the data of the socket itself.

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3])
>>> x += 1     # executed now: x = [[2 3 4]]
>>> x += 1     # executed now: x = [[3 4 5]]
>>> x *= 2     # executed now: x = [[6 8 10]]
>>> seq = spu.Sequence(x)
>>> seq.exec_seq()
>>> x

The result is [[16 20 24]] and not [[6 8 10]]: the three operations were executed a first time when they were written, then replayed by the sequence on [[6 8 10]] (6+1+1 = 8, 8×2 = 16, …).

To get the expected result, reset the data before running the sequence, for instance through a NumPy view of the socket:

>>> x = spu.array([1, 2, 3])
>>> x_view = x.numpy
>>> x += 1
>>> x += 1
>>> x *= 2
>>> seq = spu.Sequence(x)
>>> x_view[:] = [1, 2, 3]   # restore the initial values
>>> seq.exec_seq()
>>> x.numpy
array([[ 6,  8, 10]], dtype=int64)

docs.title: Process several frames at once
docs.text:
Socket data is 2D: one row per frame. By default a task processes one frame per execution. Setting n_frames on the sequence makes each execution process several frames, which reduces the overhead per frame:

>>> seq = spu.Sequence(out)
>>> seq.n_frames = 4
>>> seq.exec_seq()
>>> out.numpy.shape
(4, 8)

docs.title: Inspect a sequence
docs.text:
Two tools help to understand and tune a sequence:

  • Export the graph in the Graphviz DOT format, then render it, for instance with dot -Tsvg seq.dot -o seq.svg:

    >>> seq.export_dot("seq.dot")

  • Display statistics about the duration of each task. Statistics have to be enabled on the tasks before the execution:

    >>> for task in seq.get_tasks_per_threads()[0]:
...     task.stats = True
>>> seq.exec_n_times(1000)
>>> seq.show_stats()

See the guides Visualizing a graph and Measuring performance for more details.
